integration_note: These records extend P001-P018 without replacing them. They require product review and must not be executed as automatic physiological or safety thresholds.

policies.title: Treat a training block as a reviewable hypothesis
policies.decision_question: Should the coach start, continue, extend, consolidate, transition, replace, or end the current emphasis?
trigger: A planned block checkpoint is due.
The rolling plan repeatedly cannot preserve the stated objective.
A major goal, race, availability, symptom, illness, or interruption change affects the block premise.
suggested_action: Separate objective status from tolerance and exposure adequacy.
Choose one lifecycle outcome: start, continue, extend, consolidate, transition, replace, or end.
State what is preserved, what changes in the next 14 days, what remains provisional, and what observation will trigger the next review.
Use a planned date plus completion and early-review conditions; do not treat elapsed weeks alone as success or failure.
alternatives: Continue a rolling plan without an explicit block when no recurring choice is being constrained.
Use a short consolidation period when exposure was adequate but tolerance or interpretability is uncertain.
End without declaring success when the objective is no longer relevant.
do_not_apply_when: A narrow daily modification resolves the issue without changing the block premise.
Clinical warning signs require professional assessment before training redesign.
The application lacks enough baseline or exposure data to claim objective status; use unresolved status instead.
policies.rationale: Periodization theory and elite practice support structured sequencing, but no fixed block duration or model is validated for every recreational runner. Treating the block as a falsifiable, revisable coordination device preserves coherence without false physiological precision.
policies.evidence_certainty: Low-moderate for model superiority; moderate for the need to avoid rigid claims
policies.athlete_applicability: High as a planning and audit policy; exact duration remains individualized
policies.threshold_basis: No universal duration, response cutoff, or mandatory block structure
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate objective indicators, review cadence, and what counts as adequate exposure to the athlete, phase, data quality, and approved product semantics.
policies.uncertainty: The value of an explicit block depends on whether it materially constrains session selection and makes review clearer than an ongoing goal plus rolling plan.
review_triggers: New direct evidence in low-volume recreational runners
Repeated block decisions that could not distinguish exposure, adaptation, and tolerance
User finds block metadata burdensome or unhelpful
Product changes the calendar horizon or approval model

policies.title: Recalibrate intensity only from converging, comparable evidence
policies.decision_question: Is the current intensity anchor materially wrong enough to revise?
trigger: A credible race or controlled benchmark materially differs from the current anchor.
Several comparable workouts show persistent disagreement among pace, heart rate, RPE, and completion quality.
The anchor is stale relative to a meaningful training or interruption period.
suggested_action: Triangulate result, execution, effort, and context rather than converting one number mechanically.
Assign high, moderate, low, or insufficient confidence and preserve the prior anchor when evidence is ambiguous.
Use effort-based or bounded targets while confidence is low.
Change only the anchors supported by the observation; one 5K does not uniquely define every threshold or race pace.
alternatives: Collect a lower-cost repeatable benchmark under comparable conditions.
Retain the current target but widen its acceptable range and add a warm-up decision point.
Use RPE/talk test with HR or pace as secondary guardrails.
do_not_apply_when: Pain, gait change, illness, or a major recovery concern makes performance testing inappropriate.
The apparent change is explained by heat, hills, wind, surface, sensor error, pacing failure, or unusual fatigue.
The only evidence is a device estimate or one unusually fast training segment.
policies.rationale: Field methods can be useful, but protocol/model choices and individual disagreement limit interchangeability. Repeated comparable observations reduce false precision and support effort-first fallbacks.
policies.athlete_applicability: High for calibration workflow; method-specific accuracy varies
policies.threshold_basis: No universal minimum test count or percentage-change trigger
policies.calibration_needed: Define accepted protocols, comparability flags, anchor expiry behavior, and confidence transitions in the deterministic data layer.
policies.uncertainty: The exact amount of evidence needed depends on measurement reliability, decision consequence, and consistency across observations.
review_triggers: New validated field protocol relevant to the athlete's available devices
Persistent disagreement between prescribed effort and execution
Frequent anchor changes that destabilize training
A material race-performance change under credible conditions

policies.title: Do not declare nonresponse from one block or one test
policies.decision_question: Does an unchanged or worse result mean the athlete did not respond to the training?
trigger: A benchmark, race, or selected metric does not improve after a block.
The coach is considering abandoning a method because one outcome was flat or worse.
suggested_action: Classify the objective as achieved, partially achieved, unresolved, or not achieved rather than assigning a responder identity.
Audit whether exposure was sufficient and whether the test actually measured the objective.
Use repeated comparable evidence before concluding that a stable response pattern exists.
Choose extend, consolidate, transition, replace, or end based on the full objective and tolerance record.
alternatives: Repeat a lower-cost comparable test after recovery.
Use a second outcome that better matches the block objective.
End the block because priorities changed, without claiming physiological nonresponse.
do_not_apply_when: A clear adverse symptom or functional trend already justifies stopping or replacing the exposure.
The athlete deliberately did not complete the block; classify exposure as insufficient rather than nonresponse.
policies.rationale: Measurement and biological variability can dominate one pre/post comparison, and responder classifications depend heavily on analytic method. The plan should not create a durable identity from noisy evidence.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate-high for the warning; low for an exact repeat-testing requirement
policies.calibration_needed: Predefine which objective indicators, minimum exposure, and comparable observations are sufficient for each block type.
policies.uncertainty: A lack of detectable change can reflect true small response, measurement noise, insufficient exposure, poor test specificity, or confounding.
review_triggers: Repeated comparable blocks with stable adherence and no relevant change
A more reliable measurement method becomes available
The selected outcome no longer matches the athlete's goal

policies.title: Handle a goal or race change through block review, not cramming
policies.decision_question: How should a new, changed, postponed, or cancelled event affect the active plan?
trigger: A race is added, removed, reprioritized, postponed, or cancelled.
The athlete changes the primary performance goal or available preparation time.
suggested_action: Classify the event as target, supported exposure, benchmark, or optional participation.
Run a versioned block review and state what objective is retained, reduced to maintenance, replaced, or ended.
Change only the committed calendar horizon after deterministic validation and user approval; leave farther work provisional or directional.
Do not compress missing race-specific work or stack demanding sessions to compensate for limited time.
alternatives: Keep the current block and use a lower-priority race as a controlled exposure.
Treat the event as a benchmark without promising peak performance.
Decline or de-prioritize the event when prerequisites or tolerance are inadequate.
do_not_apply_when: The event has no material effect on session choice, recovery, or user expectations; record it without replacing the block.
Clinical constraints require a separate return decision first.
policies.rationale: Race specificity commonly rises near important events, but elite sequencing is descriptive and cannot justify last-minute dose transfer. An explicit review makes tradeoffs visible and prevents make-up compression.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for broad sequencing and taper principles; low for exact transition timing
policies.threshold_basis: No universal minimum preparation weeks or mandatory event-specific session count
policies.calibration_needed: Define event-priority semantics, approval behavior, and what preparation prerequisites are represented in athlete state.
policies.uncertainty: The best response depends on event priority, current fitness, recent exposure, tolerance, and the cost of changing the active objective.
review_triggers: Event date or priority changes again
Symptoms or recovery worsen during the transition
The athlete rejects the proposed tradeoff

policies.title: Taper by reducing accumulated load while retaining familiar readiness
policies.decision_question: How should training change before an important event?
trigger: An important event is close enough that reducing accumulated fatigue may improve performance.
A block review explicitly transitions into a taper.
suggested_action: Reduce total training load primarily through volume while retaining small, familiar doses of intensity and usually ordinary movement frequency when tolerated.
Remove novel or high-cost exposures and avoid trying to create missing fitness.
Individualize duration and reduction from event demands, recent load, tolerance, and prior response.
Track symptom stability, subjective freshness, and execution without reacting to one restless or flat day.
alternatives: Use a shorter or more conservative reduction when recent load is already low.
Retain only easy movement when symptoms or illness make intensity inappropriate.
Treat a lower-priority event as a supported exposure rather than creating a full taper.
do_not_apply_when: There is no important event or no accumulated load to shed.
The athlete has a clinical or illness constraint requiring different guidance.
The proposed taper introduces novel fast work, strength, terrain, equipment, or testing.
policies.rationale: Meta-analytic endurance evidence supports tapering through reduced volume with familiar intensity and often frequency maintained. Recreational marathon associations are supportive but cannot establish one optimal duration or percentage.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for the general strategy; low for an exact individual recipe
policies.athlete_applicability: Moderate-high once a real event and recent load are known
policies.threshold_basis: No universal taper duration or volume-reduction percentage
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate from event type, recent training, athlete history, current fatigue, and symptom response.
policies.uncertainty: Heterogeneity across sports and observational confounding limit precise recreational-running rules.
review_triggers: The athlete has an adverse or successful taper response to record
New sport- and population-specific taper evidence
